lesson.title: Mapping the Peaks and Valleys of a Function
lesson.summary: Applying the First Derivative Test systematically across an entire domain, rather than at one point, produces a complete inventory of a function's local maxima and minima, the backbone of accurate curve sketching.
lesson.body:
Up to now you have used the First Derivative Test as a tool for one critical number at a time: check the sign of f'(x) just to the left and just to the right, and decide whether that single point is a peak or a valley. Local extrema analysis is what happens when you stop treating that as a one time check and instead apply it systematically across an entire function, producing a complete map of where the graph climbs, where it falls, and every point where it turns around. That complete map is exactly the increasing and decreasing skeleton that curve sketching depends on, so this chapter is really about turning a tool you already know into a full workflow.

Work through a running example: f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 5. Its derivative is f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12, which factors as f'(x) = 6(x - 2)(x + 1). Since f' is a polynomial it is never undefined, so the only critical numbers come from f'(x) = 0, giving x = -1 and x = 2. Those two numbers split the real line into three intervals: (negative infinity, -1), (-1, 2), and (2, positive infinity).

Test one point in each interval. At x = -2: f'(-2) = 6(-4)(-1) = 24, positive, so f is increasing. At x = 0: f'(0) = 6(-2)(1) = -12, negative, so f is decreasing. At x = 3: f'(3) = 6(1)(4) = 24, positive, so f is increasing again. The sign pattern is plus, then minus, then plus. Because f' switches from positive to negative at x = -1, that point is a local maximum. Because f' switches from negative to positive at x = 2, that point is a local minimum. Evaluating the original function gives the actual peak and valley heights: f(-1) = 2(-1) - 3(1) + 12 + 5 = 12, and f(2) = 2(8) - 3(4) - 24 + 5 = -15.

You can cross check both classifications with the Second Derivative Test. Here f''(x) = 12x - 6. At x = -1, f''(-1) = -18, which is negative, confirming a local maximum. At x = 2, f''(2) = 18, which is positive, confirming a local minimum. The two tests agree, as they always will when the Second Derivative Test is conclusive. If f''(c) had come out to be zero at a critical number, the Second Derivative Test would tell you nothing, and you would need to fall back on the sign chart from the First Derivative Test instead.

One caution is worth building in now: a critical number is not automatically an extremum. Consider f(x) = x^3 at x = 0. Its derivative is f'(x) = 3x^2, which is zero at x = 0 but positive everywhere else, on both sides. The sign of f' never actually changes, so despite f'(0) = 0, there is no local maximum or minimum at x = 0, only a momentary flattening as the graph pauses on its way up. Finding a critical number is the first step of the analysis, never the last.

Put together, this is the payoff of local extrema analysis: a complete, verified inventory of every peak and valley a function has, exactly the backbone curve sketching needs to produce an accurate graph. It is also the exact skill that gets reused, unchanged, once you start solving applied optimization problems later in this unit, where the question shifts from what does this graph look like to what is the maximum profit, or the minimum cost, that a real situation allows.
